section.content: Techniques are described for generating and applying micro machine learning variants of machine learning algorithms to conserve computing resources when adapting and selecting machine learning algorithms. In an embodiment, at least one of the super parameter values for the reference variant is modified to a new super parameter value, thereby generating a new variant of the machine learning algorithm from the reference variant of the machine learning algorithm. Based on the cost metric of the new variant of the machine learning algorithm and comparing the performance scores of the new variant and the reference variant, the system determines whether the modified reference machine algorithm is a micro-machine learning algorithm that is computationally less costly than the reference variant of the machine learning algorithm but closely follows the accuracy of the reference variant.

描述了用于生成和应用机器学习算法的微型机器学习变体以在调整和选择机器学习算法时节省计算资源的技术。在实施例中，用于参考变体的超参数值中的至少一个超参数值被修改为新的超参数值，从而从机器学习算法的参考变体生成机器学习算法的新变体。基于机器学习算法的新变体的成本度量并将新变体和参考变体的性能得分进行比较，系统确定修改后的参考机器算法是否是计算上成本低于机器学习算法的参考变体但紧密跟随参考变体的准确度的微型机器学习算法。

Micro machine learningTechnical Field

The invention relates to the field of machine learning and deep learning of artificial intelligence, in particular to a mini-machine learning (mini-machine learning) algorithm.

Background

The approaches described in this section are approaches that could be pursued, but not necessarily approaches that have been previously conceived or pursued. Thus, unless otherwise indicated, any methods described in this section should not be construed as prior art merely by virtue of their inclusion in this section.

Machine learning techniques are now used in a wide variety of applications. Decades of research have created various algorithms and techniques that can be applied to these applications. Selecting the best algorithm for application can be difficult and can take up a significant amount of resources. For example, classification tasks may be accomplished by several algorithms, such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs), random forests, decision trees, artificial neural networks, and the like. Each of these algorithms has many variations and configurations, and performs differently on different data sets. Selecting the best algorithm is typically a manual task performed by a data scientist or machine learning expert with many years of experience.

On the other hand, if various machine learning techniques are automatically explored on the data, a large amount of computational overhead is incurred, so that it may even delay the entry of machine learning-based products into the market. Therefore, it may not be feasible to automatically train and validate every machine learning algorithm to find the best performing algorithm.

To avoid exploring every machine learning technique, automated methods of selective training typically end up using a single regressor/classifier to predict algorithm performance without the need to train or validate the algorithm. For example, such a regressor/classifier may be a "landmark" (landmark) algorithm that is applied to a data set (or samples thereof) to predict the performance of an unrelated machine learning algorithm. Landmark algorithms, such as naive bayes-type algorithms, k-nearest neighbor algorithms with one neighbor, decision stumps, or Principal Component Analysis (PCA) -based algorithms, can be used to predict the performance of neural networks, decision trees, or neural network algorithms.

However, since the machine learning algorithm using the landmark algorithm is different from the landmark algorithm itself, the accuracy of prediction is low. Thus, even though a machine learning algorithm may be selected based on landmarks, it may not actually represent the best machine learning algorithm for predicting results.

Furthermore, the landmark algorithm approach also does not take into account variations of the same algorithm, which can significantly affect the performance and behavior of the algorithm. Whether automatic algorithm selection is used or any other method is used to select a particular algorithm, the performance of the selected algorithm may vary based on variations in the same algorithm. The landmark algorithm, by itself, is different from the machine learning algorithm to be selected, and therefore cannot indicate which variant of a particular machine learning algorithm will yield higher or lower accuracy. The landmark algorithm has no information and no association with a particular machine learning algorithm and therefore cannot provide any substantial information for a variant of a particular machine algorithm.

Detailed Description

In the following description, for purposes of explanation, numerous specific details are set forth in order to provide a thorough understanding of the present invention. It will be apparent, however, that the present invention may be practiced without these specific details. In other instances, structures and devices are shown in block diagram form in order to avoid unnecessarily obscuring the present invention.

Training machine learning model

Machine learning techniques include applying a machine learning algorithm on a training data set for which the result(s) are known and having initialization parameters whose values are modified in each training iteration to more accurately produce the known result(s) (referred to herein as "tag(s)"). Based on such application(s), these techniques generate a machine learning model with known parameters. Thus, the machine learning model includes a model data representation or model artifact (artifact). The model artifact includes parameter values that are applied by a machine learning algorithm to the input to generate a predicted output. Training a machine learning model requires determining parameter values for a model workpiece. The structure and organization of the parameter values depends on the machine learning algorithm.

Thus, the term "machine learning algorithm" (or simply "algorithm") refers herein to a process or set of rules to be followed in a computation, wherein a model artifact comprising one or more parameters for the computation is unknown, while the term "machine learning model" (or simply "model") refers herein to a process or set of rules to be followed in a computation, wherein a model artifact comprising one or more parameters is known and has been derived based on training of the respective machine learning algorithm using one or more training data sets. Once trained, the input is applied to the machine learning model to make a prediction, which may also be referred to herein as a prediction result or output.

In supervised training, a supervised training algorithm uses training data to train a machine learning model. The training data includes inputs and "known" outputs, labels. In an embodiment, the supervised training algorithm is an iterative process. In each iteration, the machine learning algorithm applies the model artifact and the input to generate a prediction output. An objective function is used to calculate the error or variance between the predicted output and the known output. In effect, the output of the objective function is indicative of the accuracy of the machine-learned model based on the particular state of the model artifact in the iteration. By applying an optimization algorithm based on an objective function, the parameter values of the model workpiece can be adjusted. These iterations may be repeated until a desired accuracy is achieved or some other criteria is met.

In an embodiment, to iteratively train the algorithm to generate the training model, the training data set may be arranged such that each row of the data set is input to the machine learning algorithm, and further the corresponding actual result, the label value, of that row is stored. For example, each row of the adult income data set represents a particular adult whose results are known, such as whether the total income of that adult exceeds $ 500,000. Each column of the adult training dataset contains a digital representation of the characteristics of a particular adult (e.g., whether the adult has a university scholarly, the age of the adult), from which, when trained, the algorithm can accurately predict whether any adult (even an adult not yet described by the training dataset) has a total revenue exceeding $ 500,000.

The row values of the training data set may be provided as inputs to a machine learning algorithm and may be modified based on one or more parameters of the algorithm to produce a predicted result. The predicted result of the row is compared to the tag value and an error value is calculated from the difference. The error value for the batch is calculated in a statistical summary function using the one or more error values for the batch row. The term "loss" refers to the error value for a batch of rows.

At each training iteration, based on the calculated one or more predicted values, a corresponding loss value for that iteration is calculated. For the next training iteration, one or more parameters are modified based on the current penalty to reduce the penalty. Any number of iterations may be performed on the training data set to reduce the loss. Training iterations using the training data set may be stopped when the variation in loss between iterations is within a threshold. In other words, when the losses of the different iterations are substantially the same, the iteration is stopped.

After the training iteration, the generated machine learning model includes a machine learning algorithm with a model artifact that produces minimal losses.

For example, the adult revenue data set described above may be iterated using a Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm to train an SVM-based model for the adult revenue data set. Each row of the adult dataset is provided as an input to the SVM algorithm and the result of the SVM algorithm (the predicted result) is compared to the actual result of the row to determine the loss. Based on the loss, parameters of the SMV are modified. The next line is provided to the SVM algorithm with the modified parameters to produce the predicted result for the next line. This process may be repeated until the difference in the loss values of the previous and current iterations is below a predefined threshold, or in some embodiments, until the difference between the minimum achieved loss value and the loss of the current iteration is below a predefined threshold.

Once a machine learning model for a machine learning algorithm is determined, a new data set with unknown results may be used as input to the model to calculate the predicted result(s) for the new data set.

In a software implementation, when a machine learning model is referred to as receiving input, being executed, and/or generating output or prediction, a computer system process executing a machine learning algorithm applies a model artifact to the input to generate a predicted output. The computer system process executes the machine learning algorithm by executing software configured to cause the algorithm to execute.

Machine learning algorithms and domains

The machine learning algorithm may be selected based on the domain of the problem and the expected type of outcome required for the problem. Non-limiting examples of algorithm result types may be discrete values of problems in the classification domain, continuous values of problems in the regression domain, or anomaly detection problems in the clustering domain.

However, even for a particular domain, there are many alternatives to choose the most accurate algorithm to solve a given problem. As non-limiting examples, in the classification field, a Support Vector Machine (SVM), a Random Forest (RF), a Decision Tree (DT), a Bayesian Network (BN), a random algorithm such as a Genetic Algorithm (GA), or a connectionless topology such as an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) may be used.

The implementation of machine learning may rely on matrices, symbolic models, and hierarchical and/or associative data structures. Parameterized (i.e., configurable) implementations of the best-class machine learning algorithms can be found in open source libraries, such as TensorFlow for PythonndC + + of Google or MLpack for C + +, of Georgia's institute of technology. Shogunn is an open source C + + ML library with adapters for several programming languages, including C #, Ruby, Lua, Java, MatLab, R, and Python.

Hyper-parametric, cross-validation, and algorithm selection

One type of machine algorithm may have infinite variations based on one or more hyper-parameters. The term "hyper-parameter" refers to a parameter in the model artifact that is set prior to training of the machine algorithm model and is not modified during training of the model. In other words, the hyperparameter is a constant value that affects (or controls) the generated training model regardless of the training data set. A machine learning model having a model artifact with only the hyperparametric values set is referred to herein as a "variant of the machine learning algorithm" or simply as a "variant". Accordingly, during training of the model, different hyper-parameter values for the same type of machine learning algorithm may produce significantly different loss values on the same training data set.

For example, SVM machine learning algorithmTwo hyper-parameters are included: "C" and "gamma". The "C" hyperparameter may be set from 10-3To 105And the "gamma" hyperparameter may be set to 10-5To 103. Accordingly, there is an infinite array of "C" and "gamma" parameters that may yield different loss values for training the same adult revenue training data set.

Thus, to select the type of algorithm, or in addition to selecting the best performing variant of the algorithm, various hyper-parameter selection techniques are used to generate a unique set of hyper-parameter values. Non-limiting examples of the super parameter value selection techniques include bayesian optimization, such as gaussian processing for super parameter value selection, stochastic search, gradient-based search, grid search, manual tuning techniques, tree-structured Parzen estimator (TPE) based techniques.

Each machine learning algorithm variant is trained on a training data set using a unique set of hyper-parameter values selected based on one or more of these techniques. The test data set is used as input to a training model for calculating the predicted outcome value. The predicted result value is compared to the corresponding tag value to determine a performance score. The performance score may be calculated based on calculating an error rate of the prediction relative to the corresponding tag. For example, in the classification domain, if only 9,000 of the 10,000 inputs of the model match the input's label, then the performance score is calculated as 90%. In the non-categorical domain, the performance score may also be based on a statistical summary of the differences between the label values and the predicted outcome values.

The term "experiment" refers herein to training a machine learning algorithm using a unique set of hyper-parameter values and testing the machine learning algorithm using at least one test data set. In an embodiment, a cross-validation technique, such as k-fold cross-validation, is used to create many pairs of training and test datasets from an original training dataset. Together, each pair of datasets contains the original training dataset, but the pair partitions the original dataset differently between the training dataset and the test dataset. For each pair of data sets, a training data set is used to train a model based on the selected superset set, and a corresponding test data set is used to calculate a predicted result value using the trained model. A performance score for the pair (or fold) is calculated based on inputting the test data set to the trained machine learning model. If there are more than one pair (i.e., fold), then the performance scores are statistically aggregated (e.g., mean, minimum, maximum) to produce a final performance score for that variant of the machine learning algorithm.

Each trial is computationally very expensive because it includes multiple training iterations for a variant of the machine algorithm to generate performance scores for a unique set of over-parameter values for the machine learning algorithm. Thus, reducing the number of trials may greatly reduce the computational resources (e.g., processor time and cycles) required for the adjustments.

Furthermore, since the performance score is generated to select the most accurate algorithm variant, the more accurate the performance score itself, the more accurate the prediction relative accuracy of the generated model compared to other variants. In practice, once the machine learning algorithm and its hyper-parameter value-based variants are selected, the machine model is trained by applying the algorithm variants to the complete training data set using the techniques described above. This generated machine learning model is expected to predict the results more accurately than machine learning models of any other variant of the algorithm.

The accuracy of the performance score itself depends on how much computing resources are spent to adjust the hyper-parameters of the algorithm. Computational resources may be wasted on testing the set of hyper-parameter values that cannot yield the desired accuracy of the final model.

Similarly, adjusting those hyper-parameters for one type of algorithm that is most likely to be less accurate than another type of algorithm may cost less computing resources (or no computing resources). Accordingly, the number of trials can be reduced or eliminated for the hyper-parameters of the discounting algorithm, thereby significantly improving the performance of the computer system.

Overview of micro machine learning Algorithm

The methods herein describe generating variants of machine learning algorithms that predict the performance of more computationally expensive variants of the same type of machine learning algorithm for training. The term "reference variant of an algorithm" or simply "reference variant" refers herein to a variant of an algorithm that is more computationally expensive to train than another variant of the same type of machine learning algorithm. The term "micro machine learning algorithm variant" (or "micro ML variant") refers to a less computationally expensive variant of a machine learning algorithm to train.

In an embodiment, the system evaluates a machine learning algorithm to determine the computational cost and accuracy impact of different unique sets of hyper-parameter values. A unique set of hyper-parameter values determined to yield acceptable accuracy while reducing the computational cost of training of the algorithm is included in the micro-ML variants.

In an embodiment, accuracy and computational cost are measured compared to a reference variant of the algorithm. The reference variants are selected as baseline variants of a machine learning algorithm, which are modified to generate miniature ML variants. The micro-ML variants are generated by iterative evaluation of variants of the reference variant, and in each iteration, at least one hyper-parameter value of the reference variant is modified. The modified algorithm is evaluated using a training data set to determine a performance score and to determine a computational cost for training the modified algorithm using the training data set. Based on the computation cost and the performance score, the system determines whether to select a modified hyper-parameter value for the micro-ML variant of the algorithm — the lower the computation cost, the more likely the hyper-parameter value is to be selected.

In an embodiment, the hyper-parameter value with the smallest computational cost is selected. Selection may also be based on the performance score satisfying a performance criterion for the micro-ML variants. The performance criteria may be based on performance scores of the reference variants.

Generating reference variants of machine learning algorithms

FIG. 1 is a flow diagram that depicts a process for generating metrics for reference variants in an embodiment. In an embodiment, at step 100, the computer system selects a reference variant having a predetermined set of hyper-parameters for a particular domain. For example, based on previous experiments, it has been shown that for classification domain problems involving three or fewer input types, specific "C" and "gamma" values yield the best performance. This variant of the SVM machine learning algorithm is then selected as the reference variant to generate the miniature ML variants. At step 110, a training data set is selected for cross-validation of the reference variants, and at step 120, cross-validation of the reference variants is performed on the selected data set. In some embodiments, the reference variants may have been associated with pre-recorded performance and cost metrics for the dataset that were used to generate the micro-ML variants. For example, micro ML variants will be generated based on one or more of the openml.

In an embodiment, to obtain a performance score for a reference variant, the reference variant is cross-validated using a selected training data set that is also used to generate a miniature ML variant of the algorithm. The performance score may be calculated by statistically aggregating the individual performance scores calculated for each dataset discount verification. At step 125, if additional training data sets exist, cross-validation is similarly performed using each additional training data set to generate a corresponding performance score for each additional training data set.

In another embodiment, the reference variants are generated in a particular domain based on tuning a particular type of algorithm on one or more training data sets. Using the techniques described above, different unique sets of hyper-parameters may be used in a particular field to perform cross-validation on one or more data sets. The trial that produced the highest aggregate performance score against the training data set(s) was selected as the reference variant.

For example, continuing with FIG. 1, at step 100, one of many variants of the machine learning algorithm is selected, but such algorithm has not been designated as a reference variant. At step 110-. At step 130, the system determines whether to perform more adjustments to the hyperparametric value of the reference variant using the hyperparametric selection technique and the performance score from the cross-validation. If so, then at step 133, the system generates a new unique set of hyper-parameter values, thereby generating a new variant of the algorithm, according to the techniques described above. Step 100-125 is repeated for the new variant until, at step 130, the system determines that no further adjustment is necessary based on the generated performance score. At step 135, the machine learning algorithm with the best performance score is selected as the reference variant.

Additionally or alternatively, at step 140, a computational cost metric is generated for the reference variant regardless of the technique by which the reference variant is selected. In one embodiment, the computational cost metric may be generated by measuring a duration for generating the machine learning model via training the reference variant on a training data set. The duration may be measured based on training using predefined computing resources.

In addition to or in lieu of the duration measurement, other embodiments of generating a computational cost metric include measurements based on one or more of memory consumption, processor utilization, or I/O activity measurements.

The computational cost metric for each training data set may be recorded separately. For example, continuing with FIG. 1, at step 145, a tuple is generated for each training data set, the tuple containing the calculated cost metric and the performance score for that data set.

Micro-machine learning variants of a generating algorithm

In an embodiment, the micro ML variants are generated based on the reference variants. The hyper-parameter value(s) of the reference variant are modified to produce a miniature ML variant that is sufficiently similar in predicted outcome to the reference variant, but at the same time is less computationally expensive. In other words, a miniature ML variant is a variant of the algorithm that follows the performance of the reference variant, but is computationally cheaper when trained on the data set(s).

Fig. 2 is a flowchart depicting a process of generating a micro ML variant based on a reference variant in an embodiment. At step 200, an accuracy criterion is selected. The term "accuracy standard" refers to a standard that determines an acceptable measure of deviation between the accuracy of a miniature ML variant and the accuracy of a reference variant. In an embodiment, the accuracy criterion is based on a difference between performance scores of the reference variant and the micro-ML variant, a difference between performance score(s) of the reference variant and corresponding performance scores of the micro-ML variant. For example, the accuracy criteria may indicate that the performance scores must differ within a certain percentage of each other, or below a certain absolute value.

At step 205, a hyperparameter is selected from the reference variants to be modified to generate a new variant of the algorithm. At step 210, the value of the selected hyperparameter is modified in the reference variant, thereby generating a new variant of the algorithm.

In an embodiment, the super parameter values are modified such that less computational resources are used for training than if the reference variant were used. For example, reducing the values of the hyper-parameters of multiple layers in a neural network algorithm makes training of the neural network less computationally expensive. Similarly, reducing the value of the over-parameter representing the number of cells in the first layer of the neural network also achieves a reduction in the computational cost of the neural network algorithm.

In embodiments where the super parameter values are independent of the computational cost of the training model, the new super parameter values are selected using any of the super parameter value selection techniques described above (e.g., Bayes, random search, gradient descent).

At step 215, a training data set is selected from the plurality of training data sets to cross-validate a new variant of the algorithm that includes a new value of the hyperparametric value. The plurality of training sets that may be used for selection at step 215 are those for which there is a performance score or for which a performance score is to be calculated for the reference variant using the techniques described above. At step 220, the system performs cross-validation on the selected training data set, thereby calculating a performance score for the selected training data set.

At step 225, the calculated performance score for the selected training data set is compared to the performance score for the reference variant for the same training data set. If the performance score meets the accuracy criteria, then the process continues to step 230. If the performance score does not meet the accuracy criteria, then the process returns to step 205 or step 210. In other words, if the performance score of the selected variant of the algorithm is similar to the performance score of the reference variant for the same dataset, then the new variant qualifies as a candidate for the micro-ML variant of the algorithm.

For example, the accuracy criterion may specify a maximum 10% measured deviation for the modified algorithm. In such an example, the difference in performance score from that of the reference variant is calculated and compared to a 10% accuracy criterion. If the calculated ratio does not exceed 10%, the accuracy criterion is met. Otherwise, the accuracy criterion has failed for the variant algorithm.

In embodiments where the accuracy criterion has failed, the process determines whether to select a new value for the hyperparameter at step 210 or to select the new hyperparameter itself at step 205. The determination is based on whether the value selection for the hyper-parameter value depends on the performance score. It is expected that the super parameter value selection technique based on predicted computational cost will adversely affect the performance score.

For example, if the number of layers in a network hyper-parameter is reduced in each iteration for a neural network-based reference variant, the process will not perform an experiment that sets an even lower value for the hyper-parameter once the accuracy criterion is not met. The lower value of the hyper-parameter is expected to yield a less accurate model and thus guarantee that the accuracy criterion is not passed. Thus, the process may transition to another hyper-parameter at step 205.

In other words, if the current super parameter value is selected at step 210 in a manner that may result in a lower performance score than a previous super parameter value for the same super parameter, then similarly, the next super parameter value will result in an even lower performance score than the current super parameter value. Accordingly, failure of the accuracy criterion is also expected for the next selection of a hyper-parameter value. In this case, in order to save computational resources, the process transitions to step 205 to select a different hyper-parameter for the modified reference variant.

For modified reference variants that meet the accuracy criteria at step 225, the process transitions to step 230. At step 230, the modified reference variant is trained on the selected training data set, and followed by a cost metric for the training. For example, the duration of time required to train a corresponding model on a defined configuration of computing resources may be recorded. In one embodiment, the process may determine the type of cost metric that exists for the reference variant and measure the same for the modified algorithm.

At step 235, the cost metric(s) of the reference variant and the modified reference variant are compared against the selected training data set. If the modified cost metric for the reference variant indicates that the computational cost of training the model is lower than the reference variant, then the selected hyperparametric value continues to qualify as a miniature ML variant. For example, if the previously described training duration metric for the modified reference variant of the selected training data set is less than the same metric for the reference variant, then the selected hyperparametric value continues to qualify as a miniature ML variant of the algorithm.

In an embodiment, the modified reference variant is selected only if the cost metric(s) for each training data set indicate less resource consumption. In such embodiments, the cost metric(s) of the reference variant for each training data set are compared to the cost metric(s) of the modified reference variant for the respective data set. At step 235, if the cost metric of the modified reference variant indicates that the computational resource consumption for training is more even for a single dataset, then the hyper-parameter value is rejected for use with the micro-ML variant.

In a related embodiment, the modified reference variant must substantially improve the computational cost for training the data set to be selected. In such embodiments, if the cost metric fails to indicate an improvement in the threshold amount of computational resources used to train the data set, then the modified reference variant is rejected at step 235. For example, a threshold may be defined as an improvement of 50% or more in cost relative to a reference variant. The cost metric of the reference variant is divided by the cost metric of the modified algorithm, and if the division is equal to or greater than 50% in percentage, then the hyperparametric value qualifies as a miniature ML variant.

In another embodiment, the modified reference variant may not be rejected at step 235 unless the cost metrics of each and every selected training data set indicate that the modified reference variant is less computationally expensive. In such embodiments, at step 240, the modified hyper-parameter value may qualify if the modified hyper-parameter value-based algorithm is less costly than the reference variant for the threshold number of data sets. The threshold number may be determined based on a percentage of the total number of training data sets available for the process. For example, if the threshold percentage is 90%, then if the algorithm based on the modified hyperparametric value is less costly for 9 of the 10 training data sets, then the hyperparametric value qualifies as a miniature ML variant.

At step 245, if more than one hyper-parameter value qualifies as a hyper-parameter, the hyper-parameter value for which the modified algorithm has produced the lowest cost metric (lowest cost of computational resources) is selected for the micro-ML variant. To determine the hyperparameter value to select for the hyperparameter, the cost metrics for each hyperparameter are statistically aggregated, and the hyperparameter value with the best performance statistical aggregation cost metric (e.g., the lowest aggregation cost metric value) is selected.

In an embodiment, if no modified value for the hyperparameter qualifies for a micro-ML variant, then the original hyperparameter value of the reference variant is used for the particular hyperparameter in the micro-ML algorithm.

Fig. 3A is a graph depicting performance scores of reference variants and micro ML variants of an algorithm for multiple training data sets in an embodiment. Each point on the graph corresponds to a performance score for a particular dataset in the openml. The rows of the reference dataset overlap with the rows of the micro-ML variants, indicating the performance of the micro-ML variants to closely follow the reference variants.

Fig. 3B is a graph depicting the acceleration percentage of the same miniature ML variant in fig. 3A relative to the same reference variant in fig. 3A for a training data set in an embodiment. Each point is a percentage of the difference between the duration of training a particular data set with a reference variant and a corresponding miniature ML variant relative to the duration of training a reference variant of the same data set. As shown, the micro ML variants represent a considerable acceleration in the training model relative to the reference model for openml.

Use of micro machine learning algorithms

In an embodiment, the micro-machine learning of the algorithm is used to determine the performance of the reference variant on the data set, since the micro-machine learning variant of the algorithm is less costly than the training of the reference variant while following the performance of the reference variant. For example, rather than cross-validating multiple different reference variants against a new training dataset to determine which reference variant will perform best for the new dataset, a corresponding miniature ML variant is used for such determination. The micro-ML variants are cross-validated instead of the corresponding reference variants, which saves a lot of computational resources. Based on the computed performance scores from the cross-validation of the micro-MLs, the reference variant with the highest micro-ML variant score is selected. Accordingly, the selection process of the reference variants is performed using the corresponding micro-ML variants to save computational resources.

In another embodiment, the performance scores of micro-ML variants on a training dataset are used to train a meta-model for hyper-parameter value selection or machine algorithm selection. One or more reference variants are selected, for which the hyperparameters are adjusted or considered for algorithm selection. The generated micro-ML variants corresponding to the reference variants are identified to generate meta-feature values for the training data set. In an embodiment, the system has recorded the performance scores of the respective training data sets when generating the micro-ML variants, and therefore the performance scores can be easily used as meta-features when training the meta-model. For a training dataset for which the system does not have a performance score for a miniature ML variant, cross-validation of the miniature ML variant will be performed on the training dataset.

FIG. 4 is a flow diagram that depicts the generation of micro ML variant-based meta-feature(s) for a dataset in an embodiment. At step 410, a training data set is selected for which meta-feature(s) based on micro-ML variants are to be generated. At step 420, the micro ML variants are cross-validated on the selected training data set to generate performance scores for the micro ML variants for the training data set. If another miniature ML variant exists at step 430, the other miniature ML variant is cross-validated on the selected data set to produce another performance score until all of the miniature ML variants are cross-validated against the selected training data set. At step 440, the generated performance scores are designated as meta-features of the selected data set.

In one or more embodiments, generated meta-features based on micro-ML variants are used in training the meta-model(s) to adjust hyper-parameter values and/or select machine learning algorithms, in addition to or instead of existing meta-features of the training data set.

One such example is the scalable and efficient distributed automatic adaptation of machine learning models and deep learning models. In such an example, a gradient-based auto-tuning algorithm may be used, which includes the following three main steps. First, given a list of parameters and their ranges, which form the parameter space to be searched, one starts by running (training and evaluating) all combinations of edge values of the parameter space in parallel. Second, for each parameter in the parameter space, the (typically wide) input parameter range is reduced in parallel by using a gradient reduction method (described later). Finally, with a refined parameter space of all parameters, a simple gradient descent is performed from the optimal point in the corresponding parameter space for each parameter.

Using meta-learning for gradient-based automatic hyper-parameter optimization for machine-learning models and deep-learning models is another example of training meta-model(s) for adjusting hyper-parameter values and/or selecting machine-learning algorithms using generated meta-features based on ML variants. In such examples, techniques are provided for optimally initializing the value ranges of the machine learning algorithm hyper-parameters and other predictions based on dataset meta-features. In an embodiment for each particular hyper-parameter of the machine learning algorithm, the computer invokes a unique trained meta-model for the particular hyper-parameter based on the inferred data set to detect an improved sub-range of possible values for the particular hyper-parameter. The machine learning algorithm is configured based on the improved subrange for the possible values of the hyper-parameter. A machine learning algorithm is invoked to obtain a result. In an embodiment, gradient-based search space reduction (GSSR) finds the best value within an improved sub-range of values for a particular hyper-parameter. In an embodiment, a meta-model is trained based on data set meta-features and performance metrics from exploratory samples of the configuration hyperspace (such as by GSSR). In various embodiments, other values are optimized or intelligently predicted based on additional trained/trainable metamodels.

Automatic machine learning model selection using an algorithm-specific neural network architecture is another example of training a meta-model(s) for tuning hyper-parameter values and/or selecting a machine learning algorithm using generated meta-features based on micro-ML variants. In such examples, techniques are provided for optimally selecting a machine learning algorithm based on a prediction of performance of a trained algorithm-specific regressor. In an embodiment, the computer derives meta-feature values from the inferred dataset by deriving, for each meta-feature, a corresponding meta-feature value from the inferred dataset. For each trainable algorithm and each regression meta-model respectively associated with the algorithm, calculating a respective score by invoking the meta-model based on at least one of: a) a respective subset of meta characteristic values, and/or b) hyper-parameter values of a respective subset of hyper-parameters of the algorithm. One or more algorithms are selected based on the respective scores. Based on the inferred data set, one or more algorithms may be invoked to obtain a result. In an embodiment, the trained regressor is a differently configured artificial neural network. In an embodiment, the trained regressor is contained within an algorithm-specific ensemble. Techniques for optimal training of regressors and/or assemblages are also provided.

Using gradient-based automatic adjustments for machine learning models and deep learning models is another example of training meta-model(s) for adjusting hyper-parameter values and/or selecting machine learning algorithms using generated meta-features based on micro-ML variants. In such examples, horizontally scalable techniques are provided for efficient configuration of machine learning algorithms to achieve optimal accuracy without the need for advertised input. In an embodiment, for each particular hyper-parameter that is not a category hyper-parameter, and for each epoch in the sequence of epochs, the computer processes the particular hyper-parameter as follows. The epoch explores a hyper-parameter based on a computer-generated hyper-parameter tuple. For each tuple, a score is calculated based on the tuple. The hyper-parameter tuple contains a unique combination of values, each value contained in a current value range of a unique hyper-parameter. All values of the hyper-parameter tuple belonging to a particular hyper-parameter are unique. All values of the hyper-parameter set belonging to any other hyper-parameter remain constant during the epoch, such as the so far optimal value of this other hyper-parameter. The computer narrows the current value range of the particular hyper-parameter according to an intersection of the first score-based line and the second score-based line. The machine learning algorithm is optimally configured based on the repeatedly reduced value range of the hyper-parameter. The configured algorithm is invoked to obtain a result, such as pattern recognition or classification between multiple possible patterns.

In an embodiment, for any new data set, either hyper-parameter value selection or machine algorithm model selection is performed by applying meta-features of the new data set as inputs to the trained meta-model. The system performs cross-validation of micro-ML variants on the new data set and uses the resulting performance scores as meta-feature values. Meta-feature values of the new data set, including meta-feature values of the micro-ML variant(s), are provided as input to the meta-model. The output of the meta-model indicates the predicted best performing machine learning algorithm and/or one or more hyper-parameter values of the predicted best performing machine learning algorithm.

The miniature ML variant serves as a meta-feature, and the accuracy of the meta-model is remarkably improved due to the performance of the miniature ML variant following the corresponding reference variant. Thus, the meta-learning algorithm has accurate inputs that describe the dataset(s) performance of the various machine-learning algorithms, thus yielding a more accurate meta-model. Since micro-ML variants are less costly to train or cross-validate on a data set than reference variants, a small amount of computational cost is required to achieve improved accuracy of the meta-model.

Overview of software

FIG. 5 is a block diagram of a basic software system 500 that may be used to control the operation of the computing system 600 of FIG. 6. Software system 500 and its components, including their connections, relationships, and functions, are exemplary only, and are not meant to limit implementation of the example embodiment(s). Other software systems suitable for implementing the exemplary embodiment(s) may have different components, including components with different connections, relationships, and functionality.

A software system 500 for directing the operation of a computing system 600 is provided. Software system 500, which may be stored in system memory (RAM)606 and on a fixed storage device (e.g., hard disk or flash memory) 610, includes a kernel or Operating System (OS) 510.

OS 510 manages low-level aspects of computer operation, including managing execution of processes, memory allocation, file input and output (I/O), and device I/O. One or more application programs, represented as 502A, 502B, 502C … … 502N, may be "loaded" (e.g., transferred from fixed storage 610 into memory 606) for execution by system 500. An application or other software intended for use on computer system 600 may also be stored as a set of downloadable computer-executable instructions, for example, for downloading and installation from an internet location (e.g., a Web server, an application store, or another online service).

Software system 500 includes a Graphical User Interface (GUI)515 for receiving user commands and data in a graphical (e.g., "point and click" or "touch gesture") manner. These inputs, in turn, can be acted upon by system 500 according to instructions from operating system 510 and/or application(s) 502. GUI 515 is also used to display results of operations from OS 510 and application(s) 502, after which the user can provide additional input or terminate the session (e.g., logoff).

OS 510 may execute directly on bare hardware 520 (e.g., processor(s) 604) of computer system 600. Alternatively, a hypervisor or Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM)530 may be interposed between bare hardware 520 and OS 510. In this configuration, VMM 530 acts as a software "buffer" or virtualization layer between OS 510 and bare hardware 520 of computer system 600.

VMM 530 instantiates and runs one or more virtual machine instances ("guest computers"). Each guest machine includes a "guest" operating system (such as OS 510) and one or more applications (such as application(s) 502) designed to execute on the guest operating system. VMM 530 presents a virtual operating platform to the guest operating system and manages the execution of the guest operating system.

In some cases, VMM 530 may allow the guest operating system to run as if it were running directly on bare hardware 520 of computer system 600. In these cases, the same version of the guest operating system configured to execute directly on bare hardware 520 may also execute on VMM 530 without modification or reconfiguration. In other words, in some cases, VMM 530 may provide complete hardware and CPU virtualization to the guest operating system.

In other cases, the guest operating system may be specially designed or configured to execute on VMM 530 to improve efficiency. In these cases, the guest operating system "knows" that it is executing on the virtual machine monitor. In other words, in some cases, VMM 530 may provide para-virtualization to the guest operating system.

Computer system processes include allocation of hardware processor time and allocation of memory (physical and/or virtual) for storing instructions executed by the hardware processor, for storing data generated by the hardware processor executing the instructions, and/or for storing hardware processor state (e.g., contents of registers) between allocations of hardware processor time when the computer system processes are not running. Computer system processes run under the control of an operating system and may run under the control of other programs executing on the computer system.

Multiple threads may run within a process. Each thread also includes an allocation of hardware processing time, but shares access to memory allocated to the process. This memory is used to store processor contents between allocations when a thread is not running. The term "thread" may also be used to refer to a computer system process in which multiple threads are not running.

Such special purpose computing devices may also implement the present techniques in combination with custom hardwired logic, ASICs or FPGAs, and custom programming. A special purpose computing device may be a desktop computer system, portable computer system, handheld device, networked device, or any other device that incorporates hardwired and/or program logic to implement the techniques.

For example, FIG. 6 is a block diagram that illustrates a computer system 600 upon which an embodiment of the invention may be implemented. Computer system 600 includes a bus 602 or other communication mechanism for communicating information, and a hardware processor 604 coupled with bus 602 for processing information. Hardware processor 604 may be, for example, a general purpose microprocessor.

Computer system 600 also includes a main memory 606, such as a Random Access Memory (RAM) or other dynamic storage device, coupled to bus 602 for storing information and instructions to be executed by processor 604. Main memory 606 also may be used for storing temporary variables or other intermediate information during execution of instructions to be executed by processor 604. Such instructions, when stored in a non-transitory storage medium accessible to processor 604, render computer system 600 into a special-purpose machine customized to perform the operations specified in the instructions.

Computer system 600 also includes a Read Only Memory (ROM)608 or other static storage device coupled to bus 602 for storing static information and instructions for processor 604. A storage device 610, such as a magnetic disk or optical disk, is provided and coupled to bus 602 for storing information and instructions.

Computer system 600 may be coupled via bus 602 to a display 612, such as a Cathode Ray Tube (CRT), for displaying information to a computer user. An input device 614, including alphanumeric and other keys, is coupled to bus 602 for communicating information and command selections to processor 604. Another type of user input device is cursor control 616, such as a mouse, a trackball, or cursor direction keys for communicating direction information and command selections to processor 604 and for controlling cursor movement on display 612. Such input devices typically have two degrees of freedom in two axes, a first axis (e.g., x) and a second axis (e.g., y), to allow the device to specify positions in a plane.

Computer system 600 may implement the techniques described herein using custom hardwired logic, one or more ASICs or FPGAs, firmware, and/or program logic that, in combination with the computer system, renders computer system 600 a special-purpose machine or programs computer system 600 as a special-purpose machine. According to one embodiment, the techniques herein are performed by computer system 600 in response to processor 604 executing one or more sequences of one or more instructions contained in main memory 606. Such instructions may be read into main memory 606 from another storage medium, such as storage device 610. Execution of the sequences of instructions contained in main memory 606 causes processor 604 to perform the process steps described herein. In alternative embodiments, hard-wired circuitry may be used in place of or in combination with software instructions.

The term "storage medium" as used herein refers to any non-transitory medium that stores data and/or instructions that cause a machine to operate in a specific manner. Such storage media may include non-volatile media and/or volatile media. Non-volatile media includes, for example, optical or magnetic disks, such as storage device 610. Volatile media includes dynamic memory, such as main memory 606. Common forms of storage media include, for example, a floppy disk, a flexible disk, hard disk, solid state drive, magnetic tape, or any other magnetic data storage medium, a CD-ROM, any other optical data storage medium, any physical medium with patterns of holes, a RAM, a PROM, and EPROM, a FLASH-EPROM, NVRAM, any other memory chip or cartridge.

Storage media is distinct from but can be used in conjunction with transmission media. Transmission media participate in the transfer of information between storage media. For example, transmission media includes coaxial cables, copper wire and fiber optics, including the wires that comprise bus 602. Transmission media can also take the form of acoustic or light waves, such as those generated during radio-wave and infra-red data communications.

Various forms of media may be involved in carrying one or more sequences of one or more instructions to processor 604 for execution. For example, the instructions may initially be carried on a magnetic disk or solid state drive of a remote computer. The remote computer can load the instructions into its dynamic memory and send the instructions over a telephone line using a modem. A modem local to computer system 600 can receive the data on the telephone line and use an infra-red transmitter to convert the data to an infra-red signal. An infra-red detector can receive the data carried in the infra-red signal and appropriate circuitry can place the data on bus 602. Bus 602 carries the data to main memory 606, from which main memory 606 processor 604 retrieves and executes the instructions. The instructions received by main memory 606 may optionally be stored on storage device 610 either before or after execution by processor 604.

Computer system 600 also includes a communication interface 618 coupled to bus 602. Communication interface 618 provides a two-way data communication coupling to a network link 620, where network link 620 is connected to a local network 622. For example, communication interface 618 may be an Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN) card, a cable modem, a satellite modem, or a modem to provide a data communication connection to a corresponding type of telephone line. As another example, communication interface 618 may be a Local Area Network (LAN) card to provide a data communication connection to a compatible LAN. Wireless links may also be implemented. In any such implementation, communication interface 618 sends and receives electrical, electromagnetic or optical signals that carry digital data streams representing various types of information.

Network link 620 typically provides data communication through one or more networks to other data devices. For example, network link 620 may provide a connection through local network 622 to a host computer 624 or to data equipment operated by an Internet Service Provider (ISP) 626. ISP 626 in turn provides data communication services through the global packet data communication network now commonly referred to as the "internet" 628. Local network 622 and internet 628 both use electrical, electromagnetic or optical signals that carry digital data streams. The signals through the various networks and the signals on network link 620 and through communication interface 618, which carry the digital data to and from computer system 600, are example forms of transmission media.

Computer system 600 can send messages and receive data, including program code, through the network(s), network link 620 and communication interface 618. In the Internet example, a server 630 might transmit a requested code for an application program through Internet 628, ISP 626, local network 622 and communication interface 618.

The received code may be executed by processor 604 as it is received, and/or stored in storage device 610, or other non-volatile storage for later execution.
